Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: 4 days of very itchy, sore, red skin; requests rapid symptom relief.
- History of present illness:
  - Onset/duration: ~4 days (conflict noted: clinician initially said 3 days).
  - Distribution: chest, hands, arms (inside elbows). Patient denies face involvement. (Clinician at one point mentioned back; conflict noted.)
  - Symptoms: severe pruritus interfering with sleep and work, skin soreness, areas of cracked/dry skin. No bleeding, no pus/discharge.
  - Prior treatment for current episode: purchased and used an over-the-counter "steroid cream" last night — no improvement (strength/dose not documented). Patient has tried antihistamines recently without benefit (type/dose not documented).
  - Past similar episodes: prior diagnosis of eczema treated successfully previously with prescription topical steroid and a shower product.
- Past medical history:
  - Eczema (history of prior episodes).
  - Childhood/remote asthma — not active currently.
- Medications:
  - No regular medications reported.
  - Recent/OTC: steroid cream purchased at pharmacy last night (strength/dose not documented); antihistamine tried recently (type/dose not documented).
- Social history:
  - Age: 31 (patient stated).
  - Lives with flatmates; works full time as a project manager at a pharmaceutical company.
  - Smoking: denies.
  - Alcohol: occasional, a few beers per week.
- Allergies:
  - Denies known allergies.

Objective:
- No formal physical examination performed during this consult; no vitals recorded.
- Patient-reported/observed skin findings from history:
  - Areas involved: chest, hands, arms (inside elbows).
  - Appearance/symptoms: red, dry, cracked skin in places; very itchy and sore. No reported bleeding or purulent discharge.
- Provider statement: clinician commented the rash “appears quite familiar/consistent with eczema” (visual confirmation/documentation of exam not present in transcript).
- Investigations: none documented or performed.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Eczema (acute flare):
   - Assessment: Eczema (acute flare)
   - Differential diagnosis: Contact dermatitis; urticaria (considered if symptoms change) — (only if applicable)
   - Investigations planned: None documented
   - Treatment planned:
     - Prescribe a stronger topical steroid (strength/route/dose/frequency not documented).
     - Prescribe emollient for use in bath/shower; advise regular emollient use for 7–10 days (product/dose/frequency not documented).
     - Offer oral antihistamine (fexofenadine suggested; dose/route/frequency not documented). Patient advised different antihistamines may be tried; OTC options discussed (loratadine, chlorpheniramine/Piriton).
     - Advise keeping a diary of potential triggers (soaps, shower gels, clothing) to identify exacerbating factors.
   - Relevant referrals: None documented
   - Follow-up: Return or recontact clinician in one week if symptoms do not improve.

2. Sleep and work impairment from itch:
   - Assessment: Symptom-related functional impairment (secondary to pruritus)
   - Differential diagnosis: N/A
   - Investigations planned: None documented
   - Treatment planned:
     - Symptomatic measures as above (topical steroid, emollients, antihistamine).
     - Reassess in 1 week if inadequate control.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs; documented skin/dermatologic physical exam (morphology, extent, laterality, secondary changes); exact names, strengths, doses, routes, and frequencies for prescribed topical steroid, emollient, and fexofenadine; specific product names for emollient and prior prescription; any photographic documentation.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Onset: clinician first said “three days,” patient stated “four days.”
  - Distribution: clinician at one point mentioned back; patient did not report back involvement (patient reported chest, hands, inside elbows).
- Transcript quality: audio quality noted as suboptimal by clinician; occasional inaudible segments but overall history and plan are documented.
